Access to this action is restricted to members who hold the timesheet approval permission in the currently selected organization. The approver must also be operating within the same organization boundary as the target timesheet. If the timesheet is not in submitted status, or if the caller lacks approval authority, the request must be rejected with an appropriate validation or authorization error.

This approval action is paired with the rejection endpoint for the same resource, which must be used when the reviewer wants to return the timesheet to draft status with a rejection reason. The approval endpoint does not accept a request body because no additional reviewer input is required for the accept flow beyond the authenticated user and organization context already enforced by the application layer.
operations.name: approve
operations.specification:
Load the target timesheet by timesheetId within the current organization context, ensuring the record belongs to the active organization and is visible to the authenticated reviewer.

Authorize the caller using the timesheet approval permission. If the caller does not have approval authority, return a forbidden response. Do not allow cross-organization access even if the identifier exists elsewhere.

Validate that the timesheet is in submitted status before processing approval. If the status is draft, approved, rejected, or any non-submitted state, reject the request as an invalid state transition.

Perform the approval in a transaction:
1. Update the timesheet status to approved.
2. Persist review metadata such as the reviewer identity and approval timestamp if those columns exist in the timesheet schema.
3. Ensure the included timelogs are treated as locked by the business workflow so they cannot be modified or removed through timesheet operations after approval.
4. Create an organization activity record describing the approval decision, because the requirements state that timesheet approval activity must be recorded in organization history.

Return the updated timesheet aggregate after commit. The response should include the timesheet identity, employee reference, week boundary, status, and any review metadata needed by the UI to display the completed approval state.

Do not accept a request body. Do not implement rejection reason handling here; that belongs to the reject endpoint. Do not change the included timelogs themselves beyond applying the approval workflow constraints.

responseBody.description: The approved timesheet with updated review state and metadata.

operations.description:
Reject a submitted timesheet after review and record the reason for the decision.

This operation is used by an approver with timesheet approval permission to review a submitted weekly timesheet belonging to the currently selected organization. The timesheet header stores the organization boundary, employee ownership, weekly range, current workflow status, submission timestamp, review timestamp, reviewer reference, and rejection reason, so the rejection action updates the existing record with the reviewer metadata and the business reason for the decision.

A timesheet can only be rejected while it is in submitted status. The rejection reason is required and must be stored with the decision so the employee can understand why the weekly collection was not approved. After the rejection is recorded, the timesheet returns to a draft-ready state according to the workflow rules, while the review metadata remains available for auditability and UI feedback.

Access to this endpoint is limited to approvers in the active organization context. Employees without timesheet approval permission must not be able to use this action, and the system must also reject requests for timesheets that do not belong to the current organization or are not currently submitted. The client should use the timesheet detail or submitted-timesheet review flow before invoking this action so that it can confirm the target record is eligible for rejection.
operations.name: reject
operations.specification:
Load the timesheet by id within the current organization scope and verify that the record exists, is not deleted, and belongs to the authenticated user's selected organization.

Authorize the request only when the current actor has timesheet approval permission. If the actor lacks approval authority, return a forbidden response.

Validate that the timesheet status is submitted. If it is draft, approved, or otherwise not eligible for review, reject the command with a conflict or validation error. Validate that rejectionReason is present, trimmed, and not empty.

Apply the status transition in a transaction: set status to rejected, set reviewed_by_employee_id to the current approver's employee id, set reviewed_at to the current timestamp, and persist the provided rejection_reason. Keep submitted_at unchanged so the record retains its submission history. Update updated_at automatically.

Because the schema includes a reviewer foreign key and review timestamps, make sure the update is performed atomically to avoid partial review metadata. Return the updated timesheet record after commit so the client can show the final review state, reviewer identity, and rejection explanation.

Do not modify timelog membership in this operation; the timesheet header is only responsible for workflow metadata. If application-layer workflow logic converts the rejected item back to a draft-ready state, ensure that is represented consistently in the timesheet status field and any downstream status handling used by the service layer. Also record an activity entry only if the wider application rules require review actions to be visible in the organization activity feed.

responseBody.description: Updated timesheet after it has been rejected.

requestBody.description: Rejection reason for the submitted timesheet.

operations.description:
Retrieve the authenticated member's currently running timer session in the selected organization.

This endpoint returns the active live tracking record used while work is in progress. A timer session belongs to exactly one employee and stores the selected project, optional task, start timestamp, and optional description that explain the ongoing work. The response is limited to the current authenticated member and never exposes timer sessions owned by other employees.

The underlying timer session record is the organization-scoped work state captured in `hrm_time_tracking_timer_sessions`. The service must resolve the employee from the authenticated user and selected organization context, then locate the one active timer session for that employee. The table enforces one active session per employee through a unique constraint, so this operation represents a single-resource lookup rather than a collection query.

If the employee has no active timer, the API should respond according to the platform's standard detail-read behavior for absent resources. The caller can use the timer start, edit, stop, and discard operations to manage the live session once it exists. This endpoint is intended for member users who are working inside an organization context and need to see the timer that is currently running for them.
operations.name: at
operations.specification:
Resolve the authenticated member's current organization context and map it to the corresponding hrm_time_tracking_employees record. Query hrm_time_tracking_timer_sessions by employee id and exclude any record that has ended_at or discarded_at set, since only an active running timer should be returned here. Because the schema enforces a unique active timer per employee, the query should expect at most one row.

Join or hydrate the related project and optional task references for the response payload so the client can render the running timer without extra follow-up calls. Preserve the started_at timestamp and description exactly as stored. Do not expose other employees' records, and reject requests when the authenticated user has no employee membership in the selected organization.

Handle the empty case as the canonical "no current timer" outcome. Do not create, update, stop, or discard anything in this operation. This endpoint is strictly read-only and should be fast-path indexed by employee id because the schema already provides a unique constraint and supporting index on the employee key.

responseBody.description: The currently running timer session for the authenticated member.

operations.description:
Start a live timer session for the authenticated member in the current organization context.

This operation creates an in-progress timer work record that captures the moment the employee begins tracking time, the selected project, and an optional task and description. The timer session is separate from a finalized timelog: it represents a running work state that remains active until the employee later stops or discards it. The server records the start timestamp automatically and keeps the session associated with the selected organization and the authenticated member who initiated it.

The selected task, when provided, must belong to the selected project. The request is rejected if another active timer already exists for the same employee, because each employee can have at most one running timer at a time. This endpoint is designed for the member actor only and uses the authenticated identity and current organization context from the request session rather than accepting employee or organization identifiers in the payload.

The returned timer session can be used immediately by the client to display the active timer state, including the recorded start time and the currently tracked project context. Subsequent operations such as viewing the running timer, editing the active timer, stopping it into a timelog, or discarding it should be performed through the dedicated timer-session endpoints that operate on the current running record.
operations.name: create
operations.specification:
Implement this as a transactional create operation for a running timer session.

1. Resolve the authenticated member and current organization context from the request auth/session middleware.
2. Resolve the employee record for the current member within the selected organization; reject the request if no employee context exists.
3. Validate that the requested project belongs to the current organization and is eligible for live tracking. Reject if the project is archived/completed or otherwise unavailable for new time tracking.
4. If a task is supplied, verify that the task belongs to the selected project. Reject if the task is missing from that project.
5. Check for an existing active timer session for the same employee. If one exists and has not been stopped/discarded, reject with a conflict-style validation error.
6. Create the timer session with the server-generated start timestamp, employee reference, organization reference, project reference, optional task reference, and optional description.
7. Persist the record in a single transaction and return the created session.

Validation and edge cases:
- Do not accept employeeId, organizationId, or startTimestamp from the client.
- Enforce that only the current authenticated member can create their own timer session.
- Preserve the start timestamp once created; it is not editable by this endpoint.
- If business rules require rounding or timelog creation, those belong to the stop operation, not here.
- Return a conflict error when an active timer already exists.
- Return a validation error when the task does not belong to the chosen project.

The handler should log an activity only if the product’s activity-recording policy explicitly requires timer-start auditing; otherwise, keep this endpoint focused on timer-session creation.

responseBody.description: The newly created active timer session.

requestBody.description: Timer start inputs for the authenticated member.

operations.description:
Retrieve and update the authenticated employee’s current running timer session within the selected organization context.

This operation represents the live timer used for ongoing work tracking before the session is finalized into a timelog. The timer session stores the owning employee, the selected project, an optional task within that project, the start timestamp, and an editable description while the timer is active. The same resource is used to inspect the current timer state and to apply allowed changes while the timer continues running.

The timer is strictly isolated to the signed-in employee and to the currently selected organization context. A user can only view or modify their own active timer session, and the system must reject attempts to access another employee’s timer or a timer from a different organization. The underlying timer session record is backed by the `hrm_time_tracking_timer_sessions` table, which enforces a single active session per employee through a unique constraint on the employee foreign key.

When updating the timer, the server must validate that the selected project belongs to the current organization and that any provided task belongs to the chosen project. If the task becomes invalid after a project change, the request must be rejected unless the client supplies a compatible replacement or removes the task. The `started_at` value is immutable during running edits and must be preserved unchanged.

If the request indicates that the timer should stop, the system must close the active session by setting the completion timestamp and initiating the workflow that converts the running session into a finalized timelog with a calculated duration. If the request indicates that the timer should be discarded, the system must mark the session as discarded and ensure no timelog is produced. If the timer is not active, the operation should return the current timer state or an appropriate not-found/no-active-timer response based on the service contract.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement as the authenticated employee’s live timer context endpoint.

Service flow:
1. Resolve the authenticated member and current organization context from the request scope.
2. Load the employee record for that member within the selected organization.
3. Fetch the unique timer session by employee id using the timer session unique constraint.
4. If no session exists, return the current empty/no-active-timer response contract defined by the service layer.
5. If a session exists, allow updates only to editable running fields: project, optional task, and description, plus an action flag to stop or discard the timer.

Validation rules:
- Reject any attempt to operate outside the current employee context.
- Reject any project that does not belong to the current organization.
- Reject any task that does not belong to the selected project.
- If the project changes and the existing task no longer belongs to it, require the task to be cleared or replaced with a valid task before persisting.
- Never modify started_at during running updates.
- Enforce one active timer per employee with a uniqueness check before start or update actions.

Persistence behavior:
- For a normal edit, update only changed running fields and keep the timer active.
- For stop, set ended_at and pass the session to the timelog creation workflow so duration is calculated from started_at to stop time.
- For discard, set discarded_at and ensure no timelog is created.
- Use a transaction when stopping or discarding so the timer closure and downstream side effects remain consistent.

Error handling:
- Return forbidden when the user tries to access another employee’s timer.
- Return conflict when another active timer is unexpectedly present for the employee.
- Return validation errors for mismatched project/task combinations or organization-scoped references.

Implementation note:
- Although the endpoint is named like a list/index style operation in the namespace, this route is a single-user contextual timer resource. Keep the path and semantics centered on `/me/timer-session`, and treat the PATCH payload as the command envelope for retrieving and mutating the active timer.

responseBody.description: A paginated view of the authenticated employee’s current timer session.

requestBody.description: Editable running timer state and completion command for the authenticated employee’s active timer.

operations.description:
Stop the currently running timer for the authenticated employee and finalize the tracked work as a timelog.

This operation closes the employee's live timer session in the active organization context, calculates the elapsed work duration from the stored start timestamp to the stop moment, rounds the duration to the nearest minute, and persists a new timelog that captures the project, optional task, description, and worked time. The running timer session is then no longer treated as active.

The operation is restricted to the caller's own timer session. It does not accept a timer identifier because the system resolves the active session from the authenticated employee and organization context. This prevents one employee from stopping another employee's running timer and matches the timer-session rules that isolate live timer behavior to the employee who started it.

The newly created timelog is stored in the time-tracking data model as a finalized work record. It belongs to the same organization and employee as the running timer, references the selected project, and may reference a task only when that task still belongs to the selected project. If the active timer session cannot be found, is already stopped, or has been discarded, the request must be rejected with a business error.

This endpoint is commonly used together with the live timer view endpoint and the timelog list endpoint. A client typically reads the current running timer first, then stops it when the work session ends, and finally refreshes timelog and timesheet views to reflect the new finalized entry.
operations.name: stop
operations.specification:
Load the authenticated employee and current organization context from the request principal. Resolve the unique active timer session for that employee using hrm_time_tracking_timer_sessions.hr_time_tracking_employee_id and the absence of ended_at/discarded_at values. If no active session exists, return a not-found or conflict-style business error depending on the application error convention.

Within a single transaction, lock the active timer session row, compute the stop timestamp as the current server time, and calculate the duration in minutes using the session started_at and stop moment. Round the duration to the nearest minute according to the time-tracking requirements. Revalidate that the selected task, if present on the timer session, still belongs to the selected project before creating the timelog.

Insert a new hrm_time_tracking_timelogs row with organization_id, employee_id, project_id, optional task_id, work_date derived from the stop moment or business-defined work date normalization, duration_minutes, description copied from the running timer, and billable set according to the application's timer-to-timelog conversion rules if that flag exists in the service layer. Then update the timer session row by setting ended_at to the stop timestamp so it is no longer active. Preserve discarded_at as null for a stopped timer.

Do not allow cross-employee access. Do not accept client-supplied duration, work date, or timer identifiers. All values must be derived from the persisted timer session to prevent tampering. If the project is archived/completed or any other domain rule prevents new timelogs from being created, reject before inserting the timelog. Return the created timelog as the successful response payload.

responseBody.description: The finalized timelog created from the stopped timer session.

operations.description:
Discard the authenticated employee’s currently running timer session.

This operation ends the active live timer for the current employee in the selected organization context without converting it into a timelog. It is used when the tracked work should not be saved as a finalized time entry, and it clears the employee’s active timer state immediately after the discard is applied.

The timer session being discarded belongs to one employee and represents the running work session that stores the selected project, optional task, optional description, and start timestamp. The selected task, when present, must belong to the selected project, and the timer session must be the employee’s current active session in the current organization context. If no active timer exists, the request must fail because there is nothing to discard.

This action is restricted to the authenticated member acting on their own timer only. It must not allow one employee to discard another employee’s running session, and it must not create a timelog or any other finalized time entry. Client flows that use the live timer should typically call the current-timer retrieval operation before or after this action to refresh the UI state.

The discard behavior is part of the timer session lifecycle and is distinct from stopping a timer. Stopping converts the running session into a timelog, while discarding ends the session without saving recorded time. The operation should return the timer session representation that reflects the ended state so the client can confirm the active timer has been cleared.
operations.name: discard
operations.specification:
Resolve the authenticated member’s current organization context and look up the single active timer session for that employee.

Validate that the caller is a member, not a guest, and that the timer session belongs to the current employee context. If the employee has no active timer session, return a business-level not-found or conflict response according to existing API error conventions.

Perform the discard in a transaction: mark the active timer session as ended in the live timer workflow, clear its active-running state so it is no longer treated as the current timer, and do not create any timelog row or any other finalized work entry. Preserve the timer session’s stored project, optional task, optional description, and start timestamp as historical data if the schema stores them, but do not expose the session as running after completion.

Enforce the business rule that only one active timer exists per employee per organization context. The discard action should be idempotent only if the current timer is still active; repeated calls after the timer is already cleared should produce the same not-found/no-active-timer style error rather than silently recreating state.

Log an activity record only if the product’s activity-log rules explicitly cover timer discard actions; otherwise, do not add side effects. Ensure all reads and writes are scoped by employee and organization to prevent cross-tenant leakage.

responseBody.description: The timer session state after discard processing.

operations.description:
Retrieve an organization time report for the currently selected tenant context.

This endpoint provides summarized reporting over finalized timelog records so authorized members can review how hours are distributed across the organization. The report is based on the time entry data stored in the timelog records, including the work date, duration measured in minutes, billable flag, description, and the related employee, project, and optional task references. The report is intended for organization-wide visibility and is not limited to the caller's own records when the caller has the required reporting permission.

Access to this endpoint must be restricted to authenticated member users in the active organization context who have the report viewing permission. If the caller does not have that permission, the system must deny access and must not return organization-wide reporting data. The endpoint must always resolve data within the selected organization boundary so that time entries from other organizations are never included in the response.

The request supports structured filtering and grouping so reporting screens can analyze hours by employee, project, or task, and can further narrow results by date range, employee, project, task, and billable status. The response should return aggregated results and summary totals appropriate for dashboards, executive summaries, and operational review. It should not expose raw mutable timelog workflows, because those belong to the timelog management endpoints used for creating and editing entries.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement a reporting query over hrm_time_tracking_timelogs constrained by the authenticated user's selected organization.

Enforce report-view permission before any query execution. Resolve the current organization context from the authenticated member session and scope all queries by organization identifier. Reject requests from members lacking report access with a permission error.

Build a reporting query that aggregates finalized timelogs by the requested grouping dimension. Support grouping by employee, project, or task, and include the associated display information needed by the client for each group. Apply date range filters against the timelog date column and optional filters for employee, project, task, and billable flag. Exclude records outside the active organization and exclude any data that does not belong to the selected organization context.

Compute summary metrics such as total logged minutes and total hours, plus any grouped subtotals needed by the response schema. If pagination is supported in the request DTO, apply it after aggregation to the grouped result set rather than to raw timelog rows. Sort results deterministically, typically by group label or total duration depending on the chosen report ordering rule.

Use read-only database access only. Do not mutate timelog records, and do not depend on unrelated tables unless they are required to resolve display names for employees, projects, or tasks. If joins are needed, join only by foreign keys and keep the query compatible with organization boundaries.

Validate the request body thoroughly: date range must be coherent, grouping must be one of the supported dimensions, and any optional identifiers must belong to the current organization. Return a structured validation error for malformed ranges or unauthorized cross-organization references. If no timelogs match the criteria, return an empty result set with zeroed totals rather than an error.

responseBody.description: Paginated aggregated time report data for the selected organization.

requestBody.description: Report filters, grouping, and pagination options for the organization time report.

operations.description:
Retrieve a weekly summary report for the currently selected organization.

This report provides a week-by-week view of organizational work activity, helping authorized users review total logged hours, the number of timelogs recorded, and how many employees contributed time within the requested period. The weekly cycle follows the business rule that a timesheet and its related summary are based on a Monday-to-Sunday week, so report grouping should align with that same weekly boundary.

Access to this endpoint is restricted to members who have the report viewing permission in the current organization context. Users without that permission must not be allowed to view organization-wide reporting information. The response is intended for oversight and dashboard use, not for editing work records. It should reflect only data that belongs to the active organization and should never leak time data from another tenant.

The report should aggregate finalized time activity from the organization’s timelog records and present the result in a form suitable for weekly analysis. If a project filter is supplied, the summary should narrow to that project while still respecting the same organization boundary and weekly grouping. The endpoint is commonly used together with the organization dashboard and time report so that managers can move from high-level weekly trends to more detailed operational views.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement a report query service that reads aggregated timelog data within the current organization context and groups the results by weekly period using Monday as the start of the week and Sunday as the end.

Enforce authorization before any database access: the caller must be an authenticated member in the selected organization and must possess the report viewing permission. If the permission is absent, return a forbidden response. All filters must be scoped to the current organization; never accept organization identifiers in the request body for this endpoint.

Use the request body as a structured query object containing date range criteria and optional project scoping. Normalize the supplied range to weekly windows and validate that the range is sensible. Build an aggregate query over hrm_time_tracking_timelogs, grouping by week start/week end and counting total timelog rows, distinct employees, and summing logged duration. If the schema stores billable information or project linkage, include those values only insofar as they are needed to support the report metrics and filters. Do not return raw timelog records.

Return a report collection response with one item per week. Each item should include the week start date, week end date, total hours, timelog count, employee count, and any other summary fields supported by the report DTO. If no timelogs match, return an empty list rather than an error. Make sure the implementation is stable across time zones by applying the organization’s intended date interpretation consistently and by treating the weekly boundary as the canonical business week, not a locale-dependent calendar fragment.

Handle common edge cases explicitly: reject malformed date ranges, return an empty dataset when the range has no activity, and ensure the report never crosses organization boundaries. This endpoint is read-only and should not write to any tables, should not create audit records unless the platform has a separate reporting audit policy, and should not depend on timesheet approval state unless the business rules for the report explicitly require approved time only.

responseBody.description: Paginated weekly summary report data for the current organization.

requestBody.description: Weekly summary report filters and scope.

operations.description:
Retrieve the current member’s personal dashboard for the active organization context.

This endpoint returns a single summarized view intended for the authenticated user’s landing page. It is designed for the current member identity rather than a specific resource ID, so the route is scoped under `/me` and does not require any path parameters. The response should provide the latest available snapshot for the caller, combining personal context with organization-scoped information only from the currently selected organization.

The dashboard is a high-level operational snapshot rather than a raw list of records. It should support the member’s day-to-day overview experience by presenting summary information derived from the user’s current employee context, time activity, timesheet state, and any organization metrics that the caller is allowed to see. If the user has reporting access, organization-level summary information may be included; otherwise, the dashboard must remain limited to the user’s own data.

Access to this endpoint is for authenticated members only. The system must always honor the currently selected organization context and must not mix information from other organizations. Cross-organization access is not allowed, and any included organization-scoped data must be resolved only from the active organization associated with the session.

This endpoint is commonly used together with time-tracking and reporting views. It can serve as the first step before navigating to detailed timelog, timesheet, project, or report screens. The response should be stable, concise, and optimized for rendering a dashboard UI without requiring additional preprocessing by the client.
operations.name: at
operations.specification:
Implement as a read-only service that loads the authenticated member’s current dashboard snapshot using the active organization context from the session.

Resolve the caller’s member identity, current employee record in the selected organization, and any available personal summary data from the relevant time-tracking domain entities. Enforce organization isolation before querying any organization-scoped records. Do not accept a userId or organizationId path parameter; the session context is authoritative.

Build the dashboard response as an aggregated DTO rather than a direct entity mapping. The service may combine data from employee, timelog, timesheet, timer session, and optionally project/task summary queries, depending on what the dashboard model supports. If the caller lacks report-view permission, exclude organization-wide reporting aggregates and return only personal metrics and personal activity data. If the caller has report-view permission, additional organization-level summary widgets may be included, but still only for the active organization.

Apply efficient read queries and avoid loading unnecessary detail records. The endpoint should not mutate any data, should not create activity records, and should not start or stop timers. If no employee record exists for the current organization, return a not-found or forbidden-style business error consistent with the service’s existing authorization model. Validate that the selected organization remains accessible to the member before assembling the dashboard.

responseBody.description: Current member dashboard snapshot for the active organization.

operations.description:
Retrieve the organization’s activity log as a paginated list of historical business actions.

This endpoint returns significant activity records for the currently selected organization only. Each record represents an important business event captured for review and accountability, including the timestamp of the event, the member who performed it when available, the action type, the target entity type, the target entity identifier and label when present, and the structured details summary stored for audit review.

Access to this endpoint is limited to authenticated members with organization management permission in the active organization context. The response is strictly organization-scoped, so users cannot inspect activity records from any other organization while working in the current context. The returned list is intended to help organization managers review operational history such as employee invitations, employee deactivations, contract changes, project lifecycle changes, task status updates, timesheet submissions and reviews, and role assignment changes.

The data comes from the append-only activity record log table and should be queried using the organization identifier from the selected context, with optional filters for member, action type, target entity type, target entity identifier, and created-at range. Results should be ordered by most recent activity first, using the created_at timestamp as the primary sort key. Because the log is historical, the endpoint must not expose any write capability or allow modification of stored entries.

If no activity records match the filters, the response should return an empty page rather than inventing records. Consumers should use this endpoint together with other organization-scoped read operations when they need to investigate why an employee, project, task, contract, or timesheet changed state.
operations.name: index
operations.specification:
Implement a read-only organization activity log query against hrm_time_tracking_activity_records.

Resolve the current organization context from the authenticated member session, then verify the member has organization-management access before performing any lookup. Reject the request if the user is not in the active organization context or lacks permission to view the log.

Build a paginated query filtered by hrm_time_tracking_organization_id = currentOrganizationId. Support optional criteria for hrm_time_tracking_member_id, action_type, target_entity_type, target_entity_id, target_entity_label, details text search, and created_at date range. Use the existing indexes on organization + created_at, member + created_at, target entity + created_at, and the trigram indexes for textual search to keep log browsing responsive.

Sort results by created_at descending, and apply stable secondary ordering by id descending if needed. Return only summary data appropriate for a list view; do not include any mutation-related fields or nested mutable relations. If the caller supplies a target entity filter, ensure the query still remains organization-scoped so a matching entity from another organization is never returned.

Because activity records are append-only historical facts, there is no create/update/delete behavior here. If the filtered result set is empty, return an empty page structure with pagination metadata intact. Errors should distinguish authorization failure, invalid pagination/filter values, and context mismatch.

responseBody.description: Paginated organization activity log entries.

requestBody.description: Activity log search and pagination criteria.

operations.description:
Retrieve a single organization activity log entry by its identifier.

This operation returns one significant business action that was recorded for the currently selected organization. An activity record is a timestamped history entry that captures the acting user, the action type, the affected target entity, and supporting details so the organization can review meaningful operational changes over time.

The returned record belongs to exactly one organization and must be resolved only within the active organization context. If the requested record does not exist in the current organization, or the caller does not have organization management visibility for that organization, the system must reject the request or return a not-found result according to the application's standard access rules. The record includes the organization owner reference, optional acting member reference, action type, target entity type, optional target entity identifier, optional target label, details, and creation timestamp.

This endpoint is typically used together with the organization activity log list operation, which retrieves multiple entries for browsing and filtering. The detail endpoint is intended for reviewing one entry in full after a user has located it in the organization history view. Because activity records are historical facts rather than editable working data, this operation is read-only and does not allow modification of the stored entry.
operations.name: at
operations.specification:
Load one hrm_time_tracking_activity_records row by primary key and verify that its hrm_time_tracking_organization_id matches the caller's selected organization context before returning it.

Use a single indexed lookup on id, then enforce organization scoping in the service layer even if the record exists. If the active organization context is missing, reject the request as unauthorized or context-invalid according to the platform's auth middleware behavior. If the record exists but belongs to another organization, return not found to avoid cross-tenant disclosure.

The response should map all stored audit fields directly: id, organization reference, optional member reference, action_type, target_entity_type, target_entity_id, target_entity_label, details, and created_at. No mutation, side effects, or transaction are required. If future authorization rules require organization management permission, enforce that at the guard or policy layer before the repository call.

responseBody.description: Organization activity log entry.

numbering starts from 1, so the first page is page 1 (not 0). This value
reflects the page parameter from the request after validation and bounds
checking.

Defines the upper bound on how many records can be returned in a single

Pagination metadata containing current page position and total data
statistics.

alongside paginated list data. It enables clients to implement navigation

access.description:
Short-lived JWT access token for authenticating API requests.

This token must be included in the Authorization header using the Bearer
scheme (e.g., `Authorization: Bearer {access}`) for all endpoints requiring
authentication. The token contains encoded claims including user identity,
roles, and permissions. Typically expires within 15-60 minutes for
security; use the refresh token to obtain a new access token when expired.
access.x-autobe-specification: JWT access token. Use in Authorization header as "Bearer {access}".

refresh.description:
Long-lived refresh token for obtaining new access tokens.

Used to request new access tokens when the current access token expires,
allowing session continuation without re-authentication. Should be stored
securely and transmitted only to the token refresh endpoint. Typical
lifetime ranges from 7 to 30 days depending on security requirements.
refresh.x-autobe-specification: Refresh token for obtaining new access tokens without re-authentication.

expired_at.description:
ISO 8601 timestamp when the access token expires.

After this timestamp, the access token will be rejected by authenticated
endpoints. Clients should proactively refresh before expiration to maintain
seamless user experience. A common strategy is to refresh when remaining
time falls below 5 minutes. This timestamp is also embedded within the JWT
itself as the "exp" claim.
expired_at.x-autobe-specification: Access token expiration timestamp in ISO 8601 format.

refreshable_until.description:
ISO 8601 timestamp indicating the absolute session expiration deadline.

Represents the latest possible time the refresh token can be used. Once
this timestamp is reached, the user must fully re-authenticate with
credentials. This defines the maximum session duration regardless of
activity. If refresh token rotation is enabled, this deadline may extend
with each successful refresh.
refreshable_until.x-autobe-specification: Refresh token expiration timestamp. Re-authentication required after this time.

IAuthorizationToken.description:
JWT-based authorization token pair with expiration metadata.

Provides a complete authentication token structure containing both access and
refresh tokens along with their respective expiration timestamps. This
dual-token pattern enables secure, stateless authentication with automatic
session renewal capabilities.

The access token is short-lived for security, while the refresh token allows
obtaining new access tokens without requiring the user to re-enter
credentials. This structure is automatically included in authentication
responses across all generated backend applications.
